Assessing the Impact of Nitrogen and Phosphate Fertilizers on the 
Growth of Radishes in Simulated Martian Regolith 
 
Plant the Moon/Mars Challenge: Fall 2024 
Professional/Undergrad Division 
Team # 19035 
Miami Dade College 
Miami, FL 
 
Team Members: Saima Akter, Melvin Garcia, Ana Ruiz 
Coach: Davia Hudson-Holness

2
Introduction 
Even though Mars has an environment that may be harsh for life, scientists believe that 
besides Earth, this may be the most habitable planet in the solar system (Candanosa, 2017). Mars 
has been known to have similar attributes to Earth because according to the National Aeronautics 
and Space Administration (NASA), as billions of years ago, it was believed that Mars even had 
oceans like those found on Earth. For years, scientists have queried whether life had been 
previously established on Mars and what that could reveal about Earth’s past and future (“Humans 
to Mars,” n.d.). Engineers and scientists have been working to develop technologies that would 
one day allow life on Mars with a safe return to Earth (www.nasa.gov). In considering life on 
Mars, scientists must consider the necessities for human survival; water, shelter, oxygen and food. 
As NASA explores the possibility of life on Mars, all four basic human needs must be considered. 
This paper focuses on some of the factors to consider when growing crops in Martian regolith. 
Research has suggested that Martian soil lacks organic matter such as carbon but may have 
some essential nutrients for plants to grow. However, the levels of these nutrients are too low for 
plants to grow healthily. Martian soil also contains large quantities of chlorine in molecules called 
“perchlorates” which are very harmful for plants and people. It has also been found that Martian 
regolith may also contain very high levels of toxic metals, which could end up in the plants. 
(Kaplan, S. 2016). Besides the challenges brought to this research by the composition of Martian 
soil, there are other challenges to consider during the planting process such as increasing pH levels 
over time, compaction of the regolith when wet, and possible root decay if there is no good 
drainage. Most of these factors were considered throughout this experimentation process.

3
Theory 
There are 16 essential elements that are required for plants to flourish. Some are classified 
as macronutrients and others as micronutrients. Macronutrients are needed for plants to grow and 
reproduce. Some of the macronutrients include carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus 
and potassium amongst other elements. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are usually available to 
plants via the air, water and the soil while nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are often introduced 
using fertilizers. 
Cherry Belle Radishes were selected by the team as the crop for this research project. This 
is an ideal crop for growing on Mars as they don't take up a lot of space and do not need heavy 
fertilization. Radishes are also known to germinate in three to ten days, they can be harvested 
between three and five weeks and the entire plant is edible. Some of the challenges of growing 
crops in Martian regolith include a lack of nutrients for growth of the radishes and compaction of 
the Martian regolith when wet. To address these issues, this experiment utilized a mixture of 
Martian regolith simulant, topsoil, and perlite. Various fertilizers were also added to compensate 
for the lack of nutrients in Martian regolith. Each additive was chosen to enhance the composition 
of the Martian regolith. The chosen mix works well because the Martian regolith acts as the base, 
the topsoil and fertilizers add important nutrients that are lacking in the Martian regolith, and the 
perlite improves the soil structure. 
 Perlite is a key ingredient in gardening because it helps keep the soil airy and improves 
how it holds water. Its porous structure allows it to hold on to moisture and nutrients, which plants 
can access over time, preventing the soil from becoming too wet. This is especially useful when 
trying to improve the composition of Martian regolith to facilitate growth of crops since it doesn't 
have organic material or the natural ability to aerate like Earth’s soil (Stone Post Gardens, n.d.).

4
By mixing perlite with Martian regolith and topsoil, it improves the soil's texture and drainage, 
which should help the radish roots grow better and absorb nutrients more easily (Stone Post 
Gardens, n.d.). Additionally, perlite is also important because it prevents the soil from becoming 
too compact, which can make it harder for roots to grow. Since perlite is lightweight and full of 
tiny holes, it helps to keep the soil loose, similar to how Earth’s soil naturally stays airy (Stone 
Post Gardens, n.d.). This balanced combination creates a growing environment similar to Earth’s 
soil, making it easier to see how plants might grow in Martian conditions (Stone Post Gardens, 
n.d.). 
As Martian soil is lacking many of the key nutrients that Earth’s soil has, especially organic 
material and nitrogen, fertilizers are very important to make up for this deficiency to help plants 
grow (AES Soil, n.d.). Several types of fertilizers were used in this experiment: 
▪ 
Bone meal: This is an organic fertilizer that is high in phosphorus, which is important 
for helping radishes grow strong roots and larger bulbs (AES Soil, n.d.). 
▪ 
Super phosphate: This is another fertilizer rich in phosphorus, but it is an inorganic 
fertilizer. Super phosphate supports root growth and helps the plant transfer energy 
efficiently. This is especially important for radishes growing in nutrient-poor Martian 
soil (AES Soil, n.d.). 
▪ Worm castings: This is an organic fertilizer that is rich in nitrogen and trace minerals. 
Nitrogen is important for overall plant growth, especially for healthy and larger leaves 
development (AES Soil, n.d.). 
▪ Urea: This is an inorganic fertilizer that is high in nitrogen and is likely to boost leaf 
growth more than phosphorus-rich fertilizers. In this experiment, it may lead to bigger 
leaves, but it might not help much with bulb growth (AES Soil, n.d.).

5
By comparing these fertilizers, it will be determined how different nutrients impact radish growth 
in the Martian regolith. The hypothesis for this study is that fertilizers high in phosphorus will 
yield larger radish bulbs while fertilizers high in nitrogen will yield more leaves. 
 
Measurement Methods 
Materials 
The Cherry Belle Radish seeds used were purchased from Ohio Heirloom Seed 
(www.ohioheirloomseeds.com) located in Columbus, Ohio. The topsoil used was Miracle Gro 
Potting Plant Mix and the Martian Regolith, MGS-1, was purchased from Space Resource 
Technology. The fertilizers used were Triple Super Phosphate, Burpee Natural and Organic 
fertilizer, Urea All Natural 46-0-0 fertilizer and Harris Worm Castings fertilizer. All fertilizers 
were purchased from Amazon. Organic perlite was also used and purchased from Amazon. Soil 
mixtures were initially planted in 4-inch Hayward Planter (4 In D x 3.7 In H) plastic pots that were 
purchased from the Home Depot. 
Plants were grown indoors in a chemistry lab that had an average temperature of 68.5 °F 
± 4.2 °F and an average humidity of 67% ± 6.0 %. The temperature and humidity were monitored 
using a Govee WiFi Thermometer Hygrometer H5179 Smart Humidity Temperature Sensor. All 
plants were exposed to light emitting diode (LED) grow lights for twelve hours each day. The 
grow lights were Gooing Top LED Grow Light, 6000K Full Spectrum Clip Plant Growing Lamp 
with White Red LEDs for Indoor Plants. pH was measured weekly using an Oakton pH 700 
Benchtop meter, electrical conductivity (EC) was measured using a Vernier Conductivity Probe. 
The data was collected using a Vernier LabQuest Mini.

6
Soil preparation 
Four control samples were prepared; two consisted of 100% topsoil, a third consisted of 
100% Martian regolith and a fourth consisted of 50% Martian regolith, 25% topsoil and 25% 
perlite mixture by volume totaling 400 mL in each pot. To investigate the impact of different 
fertilizers on the growth of the radishes, phosphorus or nitrogen fertilizers were added to treatment 
pots with the 50% Martian regolith, 25% topsoil and 25% perlite mixture. The phosphorus rich 
fertilizers were bone meal and super phosphate while the nitrogen rich fertilizers were worm 
castings and urea. The amounts added were determined by the instructions on the packages. The 
added amounts of fertilizers are shown in Table 1. There were duplicate samples for each treatment 
pot resulting in an additional eight samples (Table 1). 
Measurements 
Weekly pH measurements were conducted by taking a spatula tip full of soil and mixing it 
with 40 mL of distilled water. The soil/water mixture was allowed to sit for ten minutes before the 
pH was measured. The soil samples were taken from the sides of the pots to minimize disrupting 
the seeds and eventually the plants which had germinated. The electrical conductivity (EC) was 
also measured weekly using the same soil/water mixture that was used for the pH sampling. The 
EC measurements, however, were only performed from week 3 onwards to explain the lack of 
growth. 
Once the plants began to grow, the height of the tallest plant in each pot was measured in 
centimeters, and the number of leaves on each plant was counted. At the beginning of the 
experiment, the leaf surface area was measured using a mobile application called LeafByte. 
However, as the plants grew and the number of leaves increased, measuring became difficult and 
these measurements were discontinued after the third week of growth.

7
Replanting 
After the first three weeks, not much growth was observed so new seeds were planted in 
fresh pots. The soil composition in the new pots was adjusted by increasing the proportion of 
topsoil from 25% to 40%, decreasing the perlite to 10% while keeping the Martian regolith at 50% 
with the volume of the mixture totaling 200 mL as the new pots were 3-inch plastic pots purchased 
from Amazon. After preparing the new soil mixture, the new seeds were planted, and regular 
measurements were continued. 
At the same time, new seeds were also replanted in the original pots in case some of the 
seeds from the original pots were damaged or removed during pH and EC testing. The original soil 
mixtures were kept unchanged, but fresh seeds were added to the original pots to give them another 
chance for germination. Prior to replanting the fresh seeds, the soil mixtures were un-clumped. 
Watering 
Each pot was watered twice per week with the optimal amount of water determined to be 
40 mL for the original pots and 30 mL for the replanted pots. 
Data Collection and Analysis 
Data was collected weekly and recorded in Microsoft excel and stored on the college’s one 
drive system. The weekly data collection included pH measurements, electrical conductivity 
measurements, plant height measurements and leaf surface area measurements. The leaf surface 
area measurements were discontinued as the plant growth increased.

Discussion and Conclusions 
At the beginning of the growth period, twelve pots each containing three radish seeds were 
planted. Four pots were designated as controls while the remaining eight pots served as treatment 
samples (Table 1). During the first three weeks of the grow period, growth was only observed in 
the control pots containing 100% topsoil and in treatment pot number seven, which included worm 
castings as an amendment. Notably, the plant in pot number seven did not resemble a radish plant. 
As a result, the soil in the original pots were loosened and new seeds were replanted. 
Simultaneously, new sample pots were prepared with modified topsoil, perlite and regolith ratios 
(Table 2). Since there were limited amounts of Martian regolith, duplicate samples for the modified 
ratios were not prepared.

15 
Since radishes tend to grow in soil pH between 6.0 and 7.0, the pH of the soil samples was 
monitored over the eight-week grow period with average values reported in figure 1 for the original 
samples. The 100% topsoil samples (control) had an acidic pH while the 100% Martian regolith 
(control) had a neutral pH. The mixture of 50% regolith, 25% and 25% perlite resulted in a slight 
decrease in the pH of the soil, but it was not as acidic as the 100% topsoil. Soil samples amended 
with worm castings demonstrated pH levels similar to the acidic 100% topsoil, while urea-
amended soil became more alkaline (Figure 1). The increase in soil alkalinity for the urea amended 
soil is consistent with the hydrolysis of urea by the enzyme urease which is found in soils. The 
urea is broken down to produce ammonia and carbon dioxide (Kansas State University, n.d.). 
CO(NH2)2 + H2O 2NH3 + CO2 
The ammonia then reacts with water in the soil and gets converted into ammonium ions which 
temporarily increases the soil pH (Purdue University, n.d.). 
NH3 + H2O NH4+ + OH- 
In a typical topsoil environment, microbes in the soil should oxidize the ammonium ions through 
nitrification producing hydrogen ions which will cause the soil to become acidic again. In the 
Martian regolith, where there is an absence of soil microbes, the nitrification process may be 
difficult contributing to the higher pH observed in the urea amended soil samples. 
NH4+ + 2O2 NO3- + 2H+ + H2O 
Similar trends were observed in the modified soil samples with the worm castings amended 
soil samples being acidic in nature and the urea amended soil samples maintaining higher pHs 
(Figure 2). The worm castings amendment of the modified soil samples had a lower pH than the 
original worm castings amended samples, and this is believed to be a result of the increased topsoil 
content (40% versus the original 25%).

16 
During the first three weeks of the growth period, growth was only observed in the 100% 
topsoil samples and one of the treatment samples amended with worm castings. To investigate the 
cause of this, electrical conductivity measurements were taken to determine if there were increased 
levels of salts present in the soil samples that could be preventing growth. Soil electrical 
conductivity measures the salt content in the soil and serves as an indicator of soil health. Soil EC 
that is too high or too low can hinder the growth of crops; too high increases the probability of root 
rot while too low indicates that the nutrients needed for growth are insufficient (Seeed Studio, 
2022). Radishes thrive in EC ranging from 800 to 1,800 s/cm (Atlas Scientific, n.d.). Even though 
most of the EC values for the samples fell in this range, growth was not observed in most of the 
soil samples suggesting that electrical conductivity was not playing a role in the lack of growth of 
the radish plants. 
For the original samples, during the first three weeks, steady growth was observed in the 
100% topsoil samples, plateauing after six weeks. One of the treatment samples with worm 
castings also showed steady growth but the rate of growth was less than observed with the topsoil 
samples (Figure 3). The lack of growth was attributed to the deficiency in organic matter in the 
Martian regolith and so new seeds were replanted in modified soil ratios where the volume of the 
topsoil was increased (Table 2). Simultaneously, the original soil samples which had gotten very 
claylike were loosened and new seeds planted. Within two weeks of replanting, growth was 
observed in the original pot containing the worm castings amendment and this growth remained 
steady for the remainder of the grow period. Within four weeks of replanting, the new seeds in the 
original regolith control mixture (pot number four containing 50% regolith, 25% topsoil, 25% 
perlite) began to grow but this coincided with the end of the eight-week growth period, so no 
further measurements were taken (Figure 4). For the modified soil samples, between week one and

17 
two, growth was observed in the 100% topsoil sample and the sample containing the worm castings 
amendment. The relative growth rates (RGR) of the radishes were calculated using the equation 
below to determine how the rates of growth in 100% topsoil compared to the rates of growth in 
the Martian regolith soil mixtures. 
RGR = 
ln(𝑀 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙)−ln(𝑀 𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙)
𝑇 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙−𝑇 𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙
 
Where: 
• 
M initial is the measurement at the beginning of the growing period 
• 
M final is the measurement at the growing period 
• 
T final−T initial is the total time interval (in weeks). 
The original topsoil samples showed an RGR of approximately 1.8 cm/week and the regolith 
mixture with worm castings showed a growth rate of approximately 1.4 cm/week. In the replanted 
samples with the modified ratios, the topsoil sample showed a RGR of 1.2 cm/week while the 
regolith mixture with worm castings showed a RGR of 0.9 cm/week. The RGR for the radishes in 
the topsoil was higher than for the radishes in the Martian regolith mixture. 
The hypothesis for this experiment stated that the type of fertilizer used would have 
impacted either the bulbs of the radishes or the leaves. Throughout the grow period, the amended 
samples that showed growth were the worm castings amended samples. Worm castings is a urea 
rich fertilizer, and the expectation was to have healthy large leaves which was in fact observed 
throughout the growth period for these samples (Figures 8 and 9). However, in addition to being 
nitrogen rich, it is also rich in organic matter, beneficial bacteria, enzymes and plant remnants 
making it an ideal fertilizer for Martian regolith which is lacking in organic matter. No growth was 
observed in the urea amended samples and it’s being theorized that even though rich in nitrogen,

18 
it lacks the additional material possessed by the worm castings that is needed to supplement the 
deficiency in the Martian regolith. 
The bone meal and the superphosphate fertilizers were expected to help with bulb 
development as they are both rich in phosphorus, but the plants under these conditions did not 
germinate. The bone meal amended samples developed mold throughout the growth period while 
no notable observations were made with the super phosphate amended samples. At the end of the 
growth period, the samples which grew were harvested to determine if radish bulbs had been 
formed. However, none of the plants which had germinated had a radish bulb. What was observed 
however, was that the roots of the radishes that were in the 100% topsoil were very healthy and 
well-formed while the roots of the radishes that germinated in the Martian regolith samples were 
very thin and shallow (figure 10 and 11). 
 
Upon reviewing all the data, it appears that what impacted the growth of the radishes was 
the presence of organic matter. The radishes planted in 100% topsoil germinated and flourished 
over the eight-week growth period as organic matter is consistently present in topsoil. For the 
amended samples, germination and consistent growth were only observed in the worm castings 
amended soil samples. The worm castings provided additional organic matter which may have 
contributed to the observed growth. This additional organic matter was not present in the other 
amended samples. The urea amended samples had a very high pH which was not conducive to 
plant growth, the bone meal amended samples developed mold and no activity was observed in 
the super phosphate amended samples. 
The choice of fertilizer when growing plants in Martian regolith, should be one that will 
provide organic matter to the regolith. One surprising development which was observed towards 
the end of the experiment was the growth in the Martian regolith control mixture (pot 4). The

19 
germination took longer than with the other samples but perhaps with the appropriate mixture of 
regolith to topsoil which will provide organic matter, growth is possible. This has led the team to 
believe that growth is possible in the Martian regolith even without the aid of fertilizers. However, 
since the germination period was so slow, the regolith may need some assistance in ensuring that 
the nutrients are being absorbed efficiently by the plants. The use of microbial inoculants such as 
Bradyrhizobium may be beneficial in this process. This experiment could be improved by using a 
mix of regolith, topsoil and perlite along with worm castings as a fertilizer to provide additional 
organic matter. The use of microbial inoculants can also be added to enhance the absorption of 
nutrients being provided by the topsoil and the worm casting.
